title: A New Transliteration Alphabet Brings New Evidence of Word Structure and Multiple "Languages" in the Voynich Manuscript
summary: Zattera proposes a slot-based transliteration and computational word grammar, then compares inferred word-form patterns between manuscript sections. The paper’s "grammar" means glyph ordering within tokens, not a demonstrated grammar of an underlying plaintext.
established: The study uses a concordance of several Landini-Stolfi transcriptions: disputed or doubtful characters and certain rare glyphs are marked unreadable, affecting 8,108 tokens, with 31,317 readable tokens and 5,105 word types retained.

Its computer-assisted 12-slot description covers 27,114 tokens (86.6%) and 2,617 types (51.3%); a further 3,249 tokens (10.4%) are separable into two regular forms. The paper selected the scheme for a simplicity–coverage trade-off on the analyzed text, so these figures are descriptive rather than held-out validation.

The paper reports a decision tree using four short character sequences to classify sections from differences in generated word grammars, and interprets this as evidence of structural variation beyond a single A/B distinction. This does not establish that the groups are distinct natural languages.

open.question: How does a frozen version of the 12-slot scheme generalize to held-out folios and to independent transliterations, including tokens excluded by the concordance?
open.check: Specify the slot rules using training pages, report token and type coverage separately on held-out pages, and compare with equally complex alternative grammars.

open.question: Do section predictions based on a fixed four-feature classifier persist when scribal hand and folio proximity are controlled?
open.check: Train by folio with grouped splits, report confusion and uncertainty on held-out sections and matched hands, then repeat on independent transliterations.
